name: Tripadvisor Design System
summary: A SwiftUI design-system prompt distilling Tripadvisor's white-canvas, single-green, circular-rating visual language into a build-ready starter.
description: Extracts Tripadvisor's iOS color, type, and component system — including its signature five-unit rating row and photo-forward cards — into a prompt that adapts the pattern to your own discovery or review app.

whatYouGet: A full hex-level color and type token set modeled on Tripadvisor's white-canvas, single-accent-green iOS palette
SwiftUI spec for the signature five-unit circular rating row, in read and interactive-picker modes
Photo-forward listing card and full-bleed detail-hero patterns at the exact ratios and radii used in the source app
A bottom tab bar and category-grid pattern with correct active/inactive tokens
A do's-and-don'ts list guarding the single-accent-color discipline that makes the rating unit and CTA read instantly
Accessibility guidance covering Dynamic Type scope and VoiceOver labeling per component
content.promptText:
<role>
You are a senior iOS design engineer at a boutique product studio who has spent the last several years building review-and-discovery travel apps in SwiftUI. You are known for nailing "trust through restraint": a near-monochrome UI that only spends color on the one or two things that actually need it, and you have shipped rating widgets, card feeds, and photo-led detail screens that stand up to App Store scrutiny.
</role>

<reference_data>
TRIPADVISOR-INSPIRED PALETTE
- Canvas: #FFFFFF (pure white, never tinted)
- Surface / grouped card fill: #F2F2F2
- Hairline divider: #E0E0E0
- Surface pressed: #E8E8E8
- Text primary (near-black): #000000
- Text secondary (metadata): #6B6B6B
- Text tertiary (disabled/placeholder): #9B9B9B
- Signature accent green: #34E0A1, pressed state #21C589
- Empty rating-unit gray: #D9D9D9
- Heritage gold accent (optional award variant): #C9A227
- Error red: #D6122E
- Dark mode: canvas #0F0F0F, surface #1C1C1E, text primary #FFFFFF, text secondary #A0A0A0 — signature green is unchanged across themes

TYPE SCALE (Inter as an open substitute for a proprietary humanist sans; weights only at 400/600/700)
- Large screen title: 28pt / 700 / -0.4pt tracking
- Detail hero name over photo: 24pt / 700
- Section header: 22pt / 700
- Card / place title: 17pt / 700
- Secondary card title: 16pt / 600
- Body / review copy: 15pt / 400, 1.45 line height
- Primary button label: 16pt / 700
- Secondary button label: 15pt / 600
- Metadata (counts, distance, price band): 13pt / 400, always the secondary gray
- Tab bar label: 11pt / 600
- Uppercase badge text: 11pt / 700, +0.4pt tracking
- Caption: 12pt / 400

SIGNATURE COMPONENT SPECS
- Five-unit circular rating row: each circle 16pt in list rows, 20pt in detail views, 24pt in a review-composer; 2pt gap between circles; filled = accent green, empty = #D9D9D9; supports a half-filled clip for decimal scores; trailing count set in 13pt secondary gray
- Award pill ("top rated" badge): accent-green fill, black 11pt/700 uppercase label, 4pt vertical / 10pt horizontal padding, fully rounded
- Primary CTA: fully rounded pill, accent-green fill, BLACK label text (never white — the mint is bright enough that black reads as higher contrast), 14pt vertical / 28pt horizontal padding, pressed state drops to the pressed-green token with a 0.97 scale
- Photo-led list card: 16pt corner radius on the photo block only (card itself is flush), 3:2 image ratio, save-glyph floating top-right over the photo
- Category entry tile: 2-column grid, ~168pt tall cells, 12pt gutter, F2F2F2 fill, 16pt radius, centered illustrative glyph above a 16pt/600 label
- Bottom tab bar: 56pt + safe area, translucent white material, accent-green active icon/label, secondary-gray inactive, hairline top border

SPACING / RADIUS
- 4pt base unit; scale 4-8-12-16-20-24-28-32-40-56
- Standard horizontal margin 16pt; 24pt between major sections
- Radius scale: 0 (dividers) · 8 (small chips/thumbnails) · 16 (photo cards, tiles) · 20 (sheets) · fully-rounded (CTAs, chips, search field) · circular (avatars, rating units)

MOTION
- Rating-unit fill on selection: 150ms left-to-right green wipe + a light haptic tick per unit
- Save-glyph toggle: scale 1.0 → 1.2 → 1.0 over 280ms with a success haptic
- Card press: scale to 0.98 on a damped spring, light haptic
- Detail-hero photo: 0.5x parallax under a sticky nav bar while scrolling
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. Reserve the accent green for exactly three jobs — the primary action, the active tab, and the rating units — because the studio's entire trust signal depends on green having only one meaning ("this matters"); scatter it decoratively and the rating stops popping.
2. Always set black label text on the accent-green button, never white — at this particular mint value white fails practical contrast while black reads crisp, and flipping it is the single most common regression a new contributor introduces.
3. Render ratings as circular units in a row, never five-pointed stars — the circular unit is this brand family's whole visual signature, and a star reads as a generic imitation of a different rival.
4. Keep every card's imagery full-bleed at a 3:2 ratio with a 16pt radius — cropping tighter or looser breaks the rhythm of a scrolling feed built entirely around that one ratio.
5. Cap weight usage at 400/600/700 only — no thin or black cuts — because the brand's legibility at small metadata sizes (13pt secondary text) depends on mid-weight strokes, and a thin cut disappears at that size on a bright white canvas.
6. Keep metadata (counts, distance, price tier) in the secondary gray token, never in the accent color or primary black — metadata needs to visually recede so the place name and the rating win the eye first.
7. Use short-throw, low-opacity shadows (around 6% opacity) on cards and reserve anything stronger for floating controls sitting directly over a photo — a white canvas only needs a hint of lift, and heavy shadows read as a different, heavier design language.
8. Never shrink the rating row below 16pt — it is read as a single geometric unit by users and needs to stay legible without a magnifying gesture.
</house_rules>

<the_project>
Describe your own place-discovery or review-driven app so the system above can be adapted, not copied verbatim:
- App name and one-line description:
- Primary content unit (e.g. restaurant, hotel, trail, service listing):
- Rating/scoring model you actually use (5-star, thumbs, numeric score, none):
- Photo availability — do listings reliably have user-submitted photos, or should the design lean on illustration/iconography instead:
- Primary conversion action (e.g. "Book", "Reserve a table", "Get directions", "Message host"):
- Top-level navigation destinations (list 3-5):
- Any existing brand color you must keep, if not this palette:
- Platform target (iOS only, or shared with Android/web):
</the_project>

<what_to_give_me>
1. Color and type tokens — a finished Swift `Color`/`Font` extension set adapted from the reference palette and type scale above to fit the project's actual brand color and rating model.
2. The signature rating component — a SwiftUI view rendering the primary review score in whatever unit shape fits the project (circles, stars, or a numeric badge), with a read-only display mode and, if relevant, an interactive picker mode with haptic feedback.
3. The primary listing/content card — a photo-forward card matching the 3:2 image ratio and card anatomy above, adapted to the project's actual content fields.
4. The detail-hero treatment — a full-bleed hero photo pattern with a scrim, title overlay, and floating circular controls (back/share/save), sized for the project's real content.
5. Navigation chrome — a bottom tab bar (or the project's actual primary nav) matching the token system, with clear active/inactive states.
6. A do's-and-don'ts checklist specific to the adapted system (5-8 items) so a teammate implementing screens later doesn't quietly reintroduce a second accent color or swap the rating unit shape.
7. Accessibility notes — Dynamic Type behavior per component (what scales, what stays fixed), VoiceOver labeling for the rating component, and minimum contrast checks for any text-on-accent-color combination.
</what_to_give_me>
install: Copy the prompt into Claude or your assistant of choice inside your iOS project
Fill in the <the_project> fields with your own app's content model, rating system, and brand color
Ask for the color/font tokens first, review them, then request the rating component and cards in follow-up turns
Drop the generated Color/Font extensions into a shared Theme.swift file before wiring components

name: Turo Design System
summary: A SwiftUI design-system prompt built from Turo's marketplace language: full-bleed photo heroes, a pinned booking bar, and a purple/teal color split.
description: Captures Turo's iOS visual system — near-black dark canvas, edge-to-edge photo carousels, host trust cards, and a sticky price-and-book bar — as a prompt you can retarget to any peer-to-peer rental marketplace.

whatYouGet: Color and type tokens modeled on Turo's purple-action / teal-trust dual-accent system, light and dark
A full-bleed photo hero carousel component with pill-dot pagination and floating overlay controls
A host/provider trust card pattern with verification badge, count, and response-time fields
A pinned price-and-book bar spec that never scrolls away, with a cost-breakdown sheet pattern
Search-card and multi-state map-pin patterns matching a marketplace results view
House rules protecting the single-CTA and action/trust color split as the system scales to new screens
content.promptText:
<role>
You are a staff-level iOS engineer who has built peer-to-peer marketplace apps end to end — the kind where a single photo carousel and a persistent price bar have to carry the entire trust-and-conversion job. You think in terms of "what one color means" and "what stays pinned to the bottom of the screen no matter what," and you default to a near-black dark canvas whenever full-bleed photography is the product's main asset.
</role>

<reference_data>
TURO-INSPIRED PALETTE
- Booking-action purple: #593BFB, bright/link variant #7C5CFF (for dark-canvas legibility), pressed #4A2FD6
- Trust/value teal: #5CE0B8, deep variant #1FB890 (light-mode text/pressed)
- Light canvas #FFFFFF, light surface-1 #F6F5FA, light surface-2 #FFFFFF, light divider #E6E4EF
- Dark canvas #0F0F12 (near-black, not neutral gray — chosen so photography stays punchy), dark surface-1 #1A1A1F, dark surface-2 #25252C, dark divider #2D2D35
- Text primary #15131F light / #F2F1F6 dark; secondary #6B6878 light / #A4A2B3 dark
- Rating-star gold: #FFB400 — reserved exclusively for the star glyph
- Semantic: success #1FB890 light / #5CE0B8 dark, warning #E8920C light / #F4A93A dark, error #E03A52 light / #F5536B dark

TYPE SCALE (Manrope as an open fallback for a proprietary geometric-humanist face; tabular numerals mandatory on price/count fields)
- Display: 32pt / 800
- Price hero (in the pinned bar): 26pt / 800
- Listing title: 23pt / 800
- Section header: 18pt / 700
- Body: 16pt / 400
- Card title: 15pt / 600
- Card price: 14pt / 800
- Meta line: 14pt / 400
- Tracked uppercase eyebrow/badge: 13pt / 700, +0.5pt tracking
- Caption: 12pt / 500
- Button label: 16pt / 800
- Tab label: 10pt / 600
- Inline rating number: 13pt / 700

SIGNATURE COMPONENT SPECS
- Full-bleed photo hero: edge-to-edge, no card frame, ~260pt tall on the detail screen; paginated carousel with a pill-shaped active dot (18pt wide) among 6pt inactive dots; floating 38pt circular blurred back/share/favorite controls over a thin top-only legibility scrim
- Specs strip: 3-4 compact tiles directly under the title, 12pt radius, 1pt divider border, teal-stroke leading icon, 13pt/700 value over a 10pt secondary label
- Host trust card: 14pt radius row, 46pt circular avatar (gradient + initials fallback), name + inline "ALL-STAR HOST" teal pill (star glyph, 10pt/800 uppercase), a calm 12pt secondary subline, trailing chevron
- Pinned price + booking bar: always visible at the bottom, blurred dark panel with a 0.5pt top divider; leading daily-rate figure (20pt/800) + an underlined "est. total" link in teal that opens a breakdown sheet; trailing purple CTA, 10pt radius
- Search/listing card: photo top (~110pt), 14pt radius, favorite heart top-right (white outline / teal filled), title 13pt/700, gold-star rating line, price 14pt/800
- Map price pin: pill shape, purple fill/white text by default; a visited pin desaturates to the surface tone; the selected pin fully inverts to a white pill with purple text so the eye finds it instantly

SPACING / RADIUS
- 4pt base unit; scale 4-8-12-16-20-24-32-40-48-64
- Screen inset 20pt everywhere except the photo hero, which is always 0-inset/full-bleed
- Radius scale: 0 (hero photo) · 10 (buttons) · 12 (fields/spec tiles) · 14 (cards) · 20 (sheets) · fully-rounded (chips, badges, pins) · circular (avatars, floating controls)

MOTION
- Carousel swipe: 1:1 finger tracking, active dot morphs to its pill width over 200ms, soft haptic tick at each page boundary
- Favorite tap: heart scales 1.0 → 1.25 → 1.0 over ~280ms with a teal fill cross-fade and a light haptic
- Card-to-hero transition on opening a listing: a shared-element-style expansion over ~320ms
- Map pin selection: scale to 1.12 and recolor over 150ms while the matching card scrolls into view
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. Never frame the hero photo in a card or add an inset border — the moment a frame appears around the primary photo, the "look inside the actual vehicle/space" illusion breaks, so hero photography is always literally edge-to-edge.
2. Keep exactly one loud accent purple call-to-action per screen — a marketplace with two competing purple buttons on the same screen makes users hesitate on which one is "the" next step.
3. Use the teal accent only for reassurance signals (elite-host badge, savings, a "free cancellation" note, instant-book, the saved-favorite state) and never for the main conversion button — mixing the two meanings collapses the "act vs. reassure" distinction the whole palette exists to preserve.
4. Pin the price-and-book bar to the bottom permanently, with content scrolling underneath it — burying the price mid-scroll is the single fastest way to tank a marketplace's conversion rate.
5. Give every listing a visible trust unit (host name, an elite/verified badge, a completed-transaction count, response speed) — a peer-to-peer marketplace lives or dies on whether a stranger's listing feels safe to transact with.
6. Set all price, count, and rating numerals to tabular figures — a jittering price as digits change width during a scroll or date change reads as broken, not dynamic.
7. Use a near-black (not neutral gray) dark-mode canvas specifically because full-bleed photography loses punch against a mid-gray background; the near-black keeps images looking lit rather than washed out.
8. Round cards and surfaces generously (10-14pt) and keep floating hero controls perfectly circular — a marketplace this photo-heavy reads as premium partly through consistently soft geometry, and a stray sharp corner reads as an unfinished screen.
</house_rules>

<the_project>
Describe your own peer-to-peer or asset-rental marketplace so this system can be retargeted:
- App name and what's actually being booked/shared (vehicle, space, equipment, service, etc.):
- Primary booking-action color you want to use instead of purple, if different:
- Secondary trust/reassurance color, if different from teal:
- What trust signals are available for each listing (host verification tier, review count, response time, completed-transaction count):
- Does pricing vary per day, per session, or as a flat rate — how should the sticky bar express it:
- Is there an instant-book / no-approval-needed path that deserves its own badge:
- Primary navigation tabs (list 4-5):
- Any existing typography constraint (licensed brand font, or open to Manrope-style fallback):
</the_project>

<what_to_give_me>
1. Adapted color and type tokens — Swift `Color`/`Font` extensions retargeted to the project's real booking-action and trust colors, keeping the light/dark split shown above.
2. The full-bleed photo hero component — carousel, pagination dots, and floating overlay controls, sized to the project's actual image aspect ratio.
3. The host/provider trust card — adapted fields (verification badge, count, response metric) with the same calm, generously-rounded anatomy.
4. The pinned price-and-action bar — with the project's real pricing model (per-day, per-session, flat) and an expandable cost-breakdown sheet if relevant.
5. Search result card and map pin set — photo-led card plus a three-state map pin (default / already-viewed / selected).
6. A short do's-and-don'ts list (6-8 items) specific to the adapted palette, so a future contributor doesn't blur the "one action color, one trust color" split.
7. Motion and haptic notes for the five interactions above (carousel swipe, favorite/save, listing-open transition, pin selection, CTA press), each with a concrete duration and easing so engineers implement identical feel across the team.
</what_to_give_me>
install: Paste the prompt into your assistant alongside your project's existing SwiftUI file structure
Complete the <the_project> section describing what you're actually renting or booking
Request the token set first, confirm the light/dark split works for your brand, then ask for individual components
Wire the pinned price bar into a ZStack/safeAreaInset at the screen root so it survives all scroll content

name: Uber Design System
summary: A SwiftUI design-system prompt built around Uber's map-first, monochrome-plus-functional-color visual language and its signature bottom sheet.
description: Distills Uber's iOS system — a 60%+ map viewport, black/white chrome, functional-only color, and a three-cut type system for display/UI/numerals — into a prompt adaptable to any real-time map-centric app.

whatYouGet: A monochrome-first color system with strictly functional accent colors (confirmed, caution, destructive, info)
A three-cut type system separating display headlines, UI text, and monospaced numerals
The signature bottom-sheet pattern with top-corner-only radius and multi-detent behavior
A moving-object map marker plus a looping arrival/confirmation pulse animation
Primary CTA and floating circular map-control component specs
House rules protecting the map's 60%+ screen share and the one-job-per-color discipline
content.promptText:
<role>
You are a principal iOS engineer who specializes in map-first, real-time transactional apps — the category where the map itself occupies most of the screen and the UI is a thin, disciplined layer of sheets and floating controls on top of it. You favor pure functional color (nothing decorative), monospaced numerals for anything measured or timed, and you obsess over keeping motion "restrained but confirming" rather than showy.
</role>

<reference_data>
UBER-INSPIRED PALETTE
- Brand: pure black #000000 and pure white #FFFFFF carry almost all primary chrome
- Gray ramp: 50 #F6F6F6 · 100 #EEEEEE · 200 #E5E5E5 · 400 #AFAFAF · 600 #757575 · 700 #545454 · 900 #2F2F2F · 950 #1A1A1A
- Functional-only color: green #05A357 (active/confirmed only), red #D72113 (surge/destructive only), blue #0A47FF (info/links only), amber #FFCB00 (high-surge caution only) — never decorative
- Dark canvas #0C0C0C (deliberately not pure black, to reduce OLED smear and match a dark map style); dark surface-1 #1A1A1A, dark surface-2 #2F2F2F, dark divider #3A3A3A
- Map tint tokens: light land #F2F2F2 / roads #FFFFFF / water #D9E5F2; dark land #1E1E1E / roads #2F2F2F / water #0F1B2A; route line #000000 light / #FFFFFF dark, both with an opposite-color casing stroke for legibility over any map color

TYPE SCALE — THREE DEDICATED CUTS, EACH WITH ONE JOB (a rounded/geometric brand face for Display+Text, a monospaced companion strictly for numerals)
- Display cut, 20pt and above: hero headline 36pt/700, sheet title 24pt/700
- Text cut, everything under 20pt: entry-field placeholder 18pt/500, row title 16pt/500, body 15pt/400, meta 14pt/400, uppercase label 11pt/700 (+0.6pt tracking), primary button 17pt/500, secondary button 15pt/500, tab label 11pt/500, caption 12pt/400
- Mono cut, reserved for every number: fare 16pt/500, ETA/address 14pt/500 — mono signals "this is measured data," never used for prose

SIGNATURE COMPONENT SPECS
- Primary CTA: solid black, 56pt tall, 8pt radius, white label, pressed state darkens to the 900-gray token with a 0.98 scale and a medium haptic
- Circular floating map control: 44pt, white fill, a ~12%-opacity soft shadow, 22pt glyph at 2pt stroke weight
- Entry-point input ("where to" style): 56pt tall, 8pt radius, light-gray fill, a from/to two-dot-and-dashed-line leading glyph, trailing time-based scheduling chip
- Primary bottom sheet: 3 detents (compact/medium/expanded), 16pt top-corner radius only (bottom stays flush), a small centered grabber pill, upward-only shadow
- Selectable option row (e.g. a ride-tier or plan choice): ~72pt tall, unselected = 1pt light-gray border, selected = 2pt black border + light-gray fill, trailing price in the mono cut
- Destination-style pin: solid black rounded shape with a tapered point and a soft ground-shadow ellipse beneath it
- Arrival/confirmation pulse: three concentric rings in the functional green, staggered and looping, signaling "the thing you're waiting for has arrived"

SPACING / RADIUS
- 4pt base unit; scale 4-8-12-16-20-24-32-40-56-72
- Radius scale: 0 (map, full-bleed) · 4 (small status pills) · 8 (buttons, fields, option rows) · 12 (modal inner cards) · 16 (sheet top corners only) · fully-rounded (chips, plate-style pills) · circular (avatars, floating controls, tab icons)

MOTION
- CTA press: spring scale to 0.98 with damping ~0.8, background darkens, medium haptic on release
- Sheet detent change: ~0.35s spring, damping ~0.85, snapping cleanly between states
- Option-row selection: border weight animates over ~150ms with a light haptic
- Confirmation pulse: ~1.8s ease-in-out infinite loop, rings staggered ~0.6s apart
- Route line draw-on: ~400ms ease-out stroke animation on confirmation
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. Keep the map at 60% or more of the visible viewport on every primary screen — the map is the actual product; any UI that starts competing with it for space has lost the plot.
2. Make every primary action black, never a brand color — a map-first app needs its map colors (route, pins, functional states) to be the only saturated things on screen, so the CTA itself stays neutral.
3. Route every number — price, distance, time, address — through the dedicated monospaced cut, never the regular text cut; mixing the two makes glanceable data look like ordinary prose and slows recognition.
4. Treat functional colors as locks, not palette options: green only means "confirmed/arrived," red only means "surge/destructive," blue only means "informational link," amber only means "elevated caution" — reusing any of them decoratively erodes the one job each color has.
5. Round the primary bottom sheet only on its top two corners, never all four — a sheet that's rounded on the bottom edge reads as a floating card rather than an anchored panel rising from the bottom of the device.
6. Keep every shadow whisper-quiet (roughly 8-12% opacity) except the sheet's own upward shadow, which is allowed to be the one prominent elevation moment on the whole screen — that's the one instance where "UI is lifted off the map" needs to actually read.
7. Float every map control (recenter, zoom, layer toggle) above the current sheet detent and inside the safe area — a control that gets covered by the sheet as it expands is a control the user can no longer reach mid-task.
8. Left-align all body text and never center it except in headlines or button labels — centering body copy in a data-dense, left-to-right utility app reads as decorative rather than functional.
</house_rules>

<the_project>
Describe your own real-time, map-centric app so this system can be retargeted:
- App name and core loop (e.g. on-demand delivery tracking, roadside assistance dispatch, fleet monitoring):
- What object moves on the map (a driver, a courier, a vehicle, a technician) and what "arrival" means in your context:
- Primary conversion action equivalent to "Request/Confirm":
- Which functional states actually apply (confirmed/active, a cost-surge or demand-spike equivalent, an info/link state, a caution state) — list only the ones you truly need:
- Do you need a live route polyline, or is the map mostly static pins:
- Primary bottom-tab destinations (list 3-5):
- Any existing brand accent that must appear somewhere, even if the primary actions stay black/neutral:
</the_project>

<what_to_give_me>
1. Retargeted color tokens — Swift `Color` extensions for the neutral black/white/gray ramp plus only the functional colors the project actually needs, light and dark.
2. Three-cut type system — Font extensions for a display cut, a text/UI cut, and a monospaced numerals cut, with guidance on exactly which fields route through which cut.
3. The primary bottom sheet — a SwiftUI sheet component with the project's real detents, top-corner-only radius, and a grabber.
4. The moving-object marker and confirmation-state animation — adapted to what "the thing you're tracking" is in this app (driver, courier, vehicle), including the pulsing arrival state if relevant.
5. The primary CTA and a floating circular map control — both at the exact padding/radius/press-state spec above.
6. A do's-and-don'ts list (6-8 items) enforcing the "map gets the room, colors are functional-only, numbers are always monospaced" discipline for future screens.
7. Accessibility notes — VoiceOver phrasing for the map marker/pin, Dynamic Type scope (which text scales vs. stays fixed for layout), and reduced-motion fallbacks for the pulse and route-draw animations.
</what_to_give_me>
install: Paste the prompt into your assistant with your MapKit or map-SDK setup already scaffolded
Fill in <the_project> with what actually moves on your map and what your functional states are
Ask for the bottom sheet and marker first — they're the two components everything else anchors to
Verify the map still occupies 60%+ of the viewport once real content and safe-area insets are in place

name: United Airlines Design System
summary: A SwiftUI design-system prompt built from United's two-blue, detail-rich flight-and-boarding-pass visual language, including its interactive seat map.
description: Extracts United's iOS system — brand navy vs. electric action blue, a tearable-feeling digital boarding pass, and a color-coded interactive seat map — into a prompt adaptable to any travel or transit app.

whatYouGet: A two-color brand token set separating brand/surface navy from an electric interactive-action blue
A boarding-pass component with a perforated tear-divider and a dark-mode-safe barcode
An interactive seat map with distinct available/premium/taken/selected visual states
A full-bleed journey-detail header pattern with route and timing information
A flight/departure status-chip set kept independent from the brand colors
House rules preserving the two-blue job split and the loyalty-gold-is-not-decorative rule
content.promptText:
<role>
You are a senior iOS design engineer who has built airline and transit apps where the boarding pass and an interactive seat map are the two screens that actually get used at the airport. You think in terms of "what has to be readable at a glance under travel stress" — airport codes, gate numbers, seat letters — and you know how to make a digital pass feel like a real, tearable artifact instead of a plain data card.
</role>

<reference_data>
UNITED-INSPIRED PALETTE — A DELIBERATE TWO-BLUE SPLIT
- Brand/surface navy: #002244 (headers, gradients, the boarding-pass banner — never used for buttons)
- Secondary navy for interactive elements on dark surfaces: #1B3D6E
- Electric action blue (the ONE interactive accent): #1414FF, pressed #0E0EC8, brightened for dark-mode legibility #4A4AFF
- Elite-status gold (reserved strictly for loyalty-tier signals): #C2A14D, bright variant #D8B863
- Light canvas #FFFFFF, surface gray #F3F5FA, divider #D4DCE9
- Dark canvas #0A1424 — a deep navy, deliberately not neutral black, so the brand navy still reads in dark mode; dark surface-1 #111E33, surface-2 #1A2A45, divider #243652
- Flight-status functional colors, kept independent of the two brand blues: on-time #1E8E5A/#4FD18C, boarding #1414FF/#7A7AFF, delayed #C98A1E/#E0A943, canceled #D8434F/#F0808A

TYPE SCALE (Open Sans as an open fallback for a proprietary corporate humanist sans; tabular numerals mandatory on gate/seat/time/mileage fields)
- Route/airport code: 32pt / 800, tight tracking (-0.5pt) — the single biggest, boldest glyph in the app
- Screen title: 26pt / 800
- Section header: 22pt / 700
- Passenger name: 18pt / 700, rendered uppercase
- Large data value (gate/seat/boards cell): 22pt / 800
- Body: 16pt / 400
- Inline data value: 15pt / 600
- Meta line: 14pt / 400
- Uppercase eyebrow/cell label: 12pt / 700 (eyebrow) and 10pt / 700 (cell label), both +0.6pt tracking
- Button: 16pt / 700
- Tab label: 10pt / 600
- Status pill: 12pt / 700

SIGNATURE COMPONENT SPECS
- Boarding pass: 16pt-radius card; a solid navy header band carrying a globe mark + wordmark on the leading side and a gold "tier · boarding-group" readout on the trailing side; a passenger row (uppercase name); a three-cell data grid for Gate / Seat / Boards, each cell a small uppercase label over a large bold value, with the Boards value rendered in the gold accent; a perforated dashed divider with two circular notch cut-outs at its edges — the "tear here" affordance; a high-contrast barcode block that inverts to a light bar pattern in dark mode so a gate scanner still reads it
- Interactive seat map: a 7-column cabin grid (3 seats, an aisle gap, 3 seats), 6pt gaps; a standard seat cell has soft top corners only; a premium-economy-equivalent seat gets a translucent action-blue tint; a taken seat recesses to the dark canvas tone; the selected seat is a solid action-blue fill with a bright glow ring; tapping springs the cell and fires a light haptic
- Flight-detail header: a full-bleed navy-to-near-black gradient; an uppercase flight-number eyebrow; a route row with large airport codes on both ends and a centered aircraft glyph + duration; a times row with departure/gate on one side and arrival/terminal on the other
- Loyalty-tier badge: a softly gold-gradient chip with a circular ring carrying the tier's short code, plus the tier name in gold text
- Status chip: fully-rounded pill, tinted background matching whichever flight-status color applies

SPACING / RADIUS
- 4pt base unit; scale 4-8-12-16-20-24-32-40-48-64
- Radius scale is deliberately CRISP: 0 (full-bleed headers, barcode edges) · 3 (seat-cell bottom corners) · 4 (buttons, fields, segmented control — the brand's signature low-radius button) · 8 (badges, inner chips) · 12-16 (cards, the boarding pass, the seat-map card) · fully-rounded (status chips, wallet-add pill) · circular (perforation notches, loyalty ring, avatars)

MOTION
- Aircraft glyph glide on the flight-detail header appearing: ease-in-out over roughly 900ms
- Seat selection: spring from a smaller scale up to full size over ~200ms, plus a light haptic
- Status change: cross-fade over ~250ms with a soft haptic, affected detail rows re-color over ~300ms
- Boarding-pass full-screen open: spring scale-up paired with an automatic screen-brightness boost (restored on dismiss)
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. Never swap the two blues' jobs — the deep navy is brand and surface only (headers, gradients, the pass banner); the electric blue is the only interactive accent (buttons, the selected seat, the active tab). Using navy for a button or electric blue for a header background breaks the "which blue means what" mental model instantly.
2. Reserve the gold accent strictly for loyalty/elite-status and boarding-priority signals — treating it as a general decorative accent dilutes the one signal it's supposed to carry: "this traveler has status."
3. Size airport codes, gate numbers, seat letters, and departure/arrival times at the largest, boldest weight available — these are read under time pressure in a crowded terminal, and anything smaller or lighter fails the "glance test."
4. Always render the boarding pass with its perforated divider and circular notch cut-outs — removing this detail turns a recognizable physical-feeling artifact into a generic data card, which is a real loss of brand identity, not just decoration.
5. Keep functional flight-status colors (on-time/boarding/delayed/canceled) completely separate from the two brand blues — a status pill that visually blends with "the action button color" makes users second-guess whether a blue pill is clickable or just informational.
6. Use a deep navy dark-mode canvas, never a neutral black — pure black makes the brand navy indistinguishable from the background and the whole "premium navy" identity disappears in dark mode.
7. Invert the boarding-pass barcode to a light bar pattern specifically in dark mode — a dark-mode barcode rendered at low contrast literally fails to scan at a real airport gate, which is a functional bug, not a cosmetic one.
8. Keep buttons and fields at a crisp, low corner radius (around 4pt) rather than the fully-rounded pill style used elsewhere in travel apps — this brand's signature is a more structured, less playful geometry that matches its "premium and precise" tone.
</house_rules>

<the_project>
Describe your own travel/transit app so this system can be retargeted:
- App name and mode of travel (air, rail, bus, ferry, etc.):
- What the two-color brand split should be in your case (a brand/surface color plus a distinct interactive-action color), if different from navy/electric-blue:
- Do you have a loyalty or elite-tier program that needs its own accent color and badge:
- What data appears on your version of a "boarding pass" (gate/seat equivalent — could be platform/coach/seat, or dock/cabin/deck):
- Do you need an interactive seat or berth map, and if so what are its occupancy states (available, premium, taken, selected):
- What flight/departure-status values do you actually track (on-time, delayed, canceled, boarding, gate-changed, or your own equivalents):
- Primary bottom-tab destinations (list 4-5):
</the_project>

<what_to_give_me>
1. Retargeted two-color token set — Swift `Color`/`Font` extensions for your brand/surface color, your interactive-action color, and your loyalty accent (if any), light and dark.
2. The boarding-pass-equivalent component — header band, passenger/traveler row, a data-cell grid for your real gate/seat/boarding-time equivalents, the perforated "tear here" divider, and a scannable code block with a dark-mode-safe inversion.
3. The interactive seat/berth map — adapted occupancy states and the selection interaction with its spring animation and haptic.
4. The journey-detail header — a full-bleed brand-gradient header with route/leg information sized for your actual travel mode.
5. A status-chip set for your real departure/arrival states, kept visually distinct from the interactive-action color.
6. A do's-and-don'ts list (6-8 items) protecting the two-color split and the "gate/seat/time data is always the biggest, boldest text" rule.
7. Accessibility notes — Dynamic Type scope per component, VoiceOver phrasing for the pass and the seat map, and the screen-brightness-boost behavior for the full-screen pass view.
</what_to_give_me>
install: Paste the prompt into your assistant with your travel app's data model already sketched
Fill in <the_project> with your real travel mode and its gate/seat/boarding equivalents
Request the boarding-pass component first since most other screens link out to it
Test the barcode/QR inversion in dark mode on a real device before shipping — contrast failures here are functional, not cosmetic

name: Vrbo Design System
summary: A SwiftUI design-system prompt built from Vrbo's photo-first, price-forward marketplace language, including its sticky booking bar and gold-accented map pins.
description: Captures Vrbo's iOS system — a full-bleed swipeable photo gallery, a permanently pinned price-and-book bar, and a single-gold-accent rating system — as a prompt adaptable to any property or asset marketplace.

whatYouGet: Color and type tokens built on Vrbo's system-font-first, single-warm-accent visual approach
A full-bleed swipeable photo gallery component with dot progress and a photo-counter pill
A sticky price-and-book bar pattern that never scrolls out of view, with a cost-breakdown sheet
A results/listing card and a three-state map price pin (default, viewed, selected)
A saved-collection ('trip board') card pattern
House rules protecting the single-gold-accent rule and the always-visible-price discipline
content.promptText:
<role>
You are a senior iOS engineer specializing in whole-property vacation-rental and marketplace apps, the kind where a full-bleed photo gallery has to sell an entire house before the user reads a single word of copy, and a persistent price bar has to survive an entire scroll session. You default to the system font and full Dynamic Type support rather than a custom typeface, and you treat "the price is the loudest thing on the screen" as a non-negotiable commerce rule.
</role>

<reference_data>
VRBO-INSPIRED PALETTE
- Primary action blue: #245ABC, pressed #1B4794, brightened dark-mode variant #4F8BF0 (used for links/pins/outlines on dark — the primary button fill itself stays the deep blue in both themes)
- Supporting accent: #1D6FB8
- Light canvas #FFFFFF, surface gray #F3F5F8, surface pressed #E7EBF1, divider #E1E5EB
- Dark canvas #101317 (a cool blue-charcoal, not pure black), dark surface-1 #181C22, dark surface-2 #21262E, dark divider #2A3038
- Text primary #15181D light / #EDEFF2 dark; secondary #5A6470 light / #A3AAB4 dark
- Exactly one warm accent — a gold review star #F2B01E — constant across both themes, used only for ratings and the selected map pin
- Trust-badge colors: a top-tier host chip in the primary blue at low-opacity fill; an instant-booking chip in success green #1F9D57
- Semantic: success #1F9D57, error/destructive #E04444, warning #E8920C

TYPE SCALE (the platform's own system font, no custom typeface — Dynamic Type is respected everywhere)
- Large screen title: 32pt / 800
- Price hero (in the booking bar / on the detail screen): 26pt / 800 — one of the loudest styles on any screen
- Listing title: 21pt / 700
- Section header: 18pt / 700
- Body: 16pt / 400
- Card title: 15pt / 600
- Fact value ("4 Bedrooms" style): 16pt / 700
- Meta/subtitle: 14pt / 400
- Badge: 12pt / 700
- Button label: 16pt / 700
- Tab label: 10pt / 500
- Caption (photo counter, dot legends): 12pt / 500

SIGNATURE COMPONENT SPECS
- Full-bleed swipeable photo gallery: ~290pt tall on a standard phone, square top corners, horizontal paging with 1:1 finger tracking and a spring snap; a bottom dot-progress row where the active dot widens into a pill; a bottom-right photo-counter pill ("1 / 42" style); floating circular back/share/save overlay controls over a thin top scrim only
- Sticky booking bar: pinned to the bottom of the listing detail at all times, ~76pt tall plus safe area, blurred translucent panel with a top hairline; leading heavy price figure plus an underlined tappable date-range line; trailing full booking CTA in the primary blue
- Results/listing card: a photo block at a roughly 4:3 ratio with a rounded corner treatment and a save-heart control top-right; below it, a title, location, a gold-star rating row, and the nightly price rendered heavier than the surrounding text; always paired with a "whole property" reassurance label
- Map price pin: a rounded pill bubble — default state fills with the primary blue and white text, an already-viewed pin desaturates to a neutral surface tone, and the selected pin is the ONLY thing on the map rendered in the gold accent, so the eye finds it instantly
- Saved-collection card: a horizontal row with a small thumbnail, the property name, a facts line (location, bedroom count, sleep capacity), and a gold "saved to {collection name}" tag

SPACING / RADIUS
- 4pt base unit; scale 4-8-12-16-18-24-32-40-48
- Screen inset 18pt (slightly wider than a typical 16pt, giving photography and cards a bit more breathing room)
- Radius scale: 0 (gallery top edge, map) · 4 (inner photo frames, small chips) · 6 (trust badges) · 10 (buttons, grouped cards) · 14 (listing photo cards, sheets) · 20 (hero cards, modals) · fully-rounded (search bar, filter chips, map pins) · circular (gallery overlay controls, avatars)

MOTION
- Gallery swipe: 1:1 tracking, spring snap to the nearest photo (~250ms, high damping), active dot animates its width over ~200ms
- Booking-bar price update: the price figure cross-dissolves/counts to a new value over ~250ms when dates change
- Save-heart tap: scales 1.0 → 1.25 → 1.0 over ~280ms with a soft haptic, fill transitions to the error/heart-red tone
- Map pin selection: scale to ~1.12 and recolor to the gold accent over ~180ms while a peek card slides up
- Results-card appearance: a subtle fade plus an 8pt upward slide, lightly staggered per card
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. Never introduce a second warm or saturated accent color beyond the one gold review star — the entire visual restraint of this system depends on blue-plus-exactly-one-warm-color; adding a second saturated hue immediately competes with the star for attention.
2. Keep the booking/price bar permanently pinned and visible — a marketplace that lets its price scroll out of view is asking the user to remember a number instead of seeing it, which measurably hurts conversion.
3. Never put a shadow or card frame around gallery photography — the gallery is meant to feel like a real window onto the property, and a shadow instantly turns it back into "a UI element" instead of "the actual place."
4. Reinforce whatever the core differentiator is (in the source app, "you get the whole place, never a shared room") directly on cards and the detail screen, not just in marketing copy — a structural promise has to be visible at the point of decision, not buried in an FAQ.
5. Make the nightly/session price one of the two or three loudest text styles on every screen it appears — in a marketplace, price is the number users are actually scanning for, and if it's visually average-weight it gets skipped.
6. Use the system font and respect Dynamic Type rather than shipping a custom typeface — for a booking flow used by a very wide age range, respecting the user's own text-size preference matters more than typographic personality.
7. Keep chrome minimal: translucent bars, hairline dividers, and soft card lifts only — a marketplace this photo-dependent should never let heavy shadows or gradients compete with the actual photography for visual weight.
8. Never recolor the gold review star per theme or per brand variant — it needs to read identically in light and dark mode so a user's sense of "this is a good rating" doesn't waver between sessions.
</house_rules>

<the_project>
Describe your own property, space, or asset marketplace so this system can be retargeted:
- App name and what's being booked (a house, a venue, a piece of equipment, a workspace, etc.):
- Primary structural differentiator you want reinforced everywhere (e.g. "whole property," "verified inspected," "no cleaning fee"):
- Primary blue or brand accent you want in place of #245ABC, if different:
- Do you have host/provider trust tiers (e.g. superhost-equivalent, instant-book) that need their own badges:
- Pricing model — nightly, per-session, or flat — and how the sticky bar should express it:
- Do results need a map view with price pins, or is a list-only view sufficient:
- Primary bottom-tab destinations (list 4-5):
</the_project>

<what_to_give_me>
1. Retargeted color and type tokens — Swift `Color`/`Font` extensions using the system font and Dynamic Type, adapted to the project's real brand blue and any trust-badge colors.
2. The full-bleed photo gallery component — carousel, dot progress, photo counter, and floating overlay controls sized to the project's real image aspect ratio.
3. The sticky price-and-book bar — with the project's real pricing model and an underlined date/detail link that opens a breakdown sheet.
4. The results/listing card and a multi-state map price pin (default / viewed / selected), adapted to the project's real facts (bedrooms, capacity, or equivalent).
5. A saved-collection card pattern (the project's equivalent of a wishlist or trip board).
6. A do's-and-don'ts list (6-8 items) protecting the single-warm-accent rule and the "price is always loud, gallery never has a shadow" discipline.
7. Accessibility notes — Dynamic Type scope per component (what's fixed for layout vs. what scales), VoiceOver phrasing for the gallery and the booking bar, and a reduced-motion fallback for the price-counting and pin-selection animations.
</what_to_give_me>
install: Paste the prompt into your assistant alongside your marketplace app's existing data model
Fill in <the_project> with your real property/asset type and structural differentiator
Ask for the gallery and sticky booking bar first — nearly every other screen references them
Confirm Dynamic Type scaling on the price hero and listing title before locking layout constants

name: Waze Design System
summary: A SwiftUI design-system prompt built from Waze's cartoon-forward visual language: speech-bubble hazard reports, an arrow locator, and a dual-brand map.
description: Captures Waze's iOS system — chunky cartoon hazard speech bubbles, a directional cyan locator arrow, tinted-purple shadows, and a saturated map style — as a prompt adaptable to any gamified or community-reporting navigation app.

whatYouGet: A dual-brand-color token set (violet + cyan) with a per-category hazard-color system, brightened rather than desaturated at night
The cartoon speech-bubble alert component with a pointed tail and a spring 'pop' appearance animation
A floating action button pattern with a brand-tinted shadow and a circular category-picker wheel
A directional (non-dot) location marker with a pulsing presence ring
Next-turn hero card and bottom info-bar patterns using a tabular numeric type cut
House rules protecting the cartoon-report tone, the loud cartography, and the arrow-not-dot locator
content.promptText:
<role>
You are a senior iOS engineer who has built community-driven, gamified navigation experiences — apps where reporting a hazard is meant to feel like playing a small game rather than filing a form. You lean hard into rounded typography, saturated cartography, and chunky cartoon-style UI elements, and you know exactly which numeric fields have to stay glanceable at highway speed versus which copy can be playful.
</role>

<reference_data>
WAZE-INSPIRED PALETTE
- Brand duo: a saturated violet-purple #7E55BE (logo, route line, primary floating action button, primary CTA), deep pressed state #5B3C9A, a light tint #E8DEF5 for selected-row fills; paired with a bright cyan #33CCFF (current-location marker, informational glyphs), deep pressed cyan #0099E5
- Hazard-report color system, each color owning exactly one report category: police-report red #EF6A65, traffic-jam orange #F69833, road-closure yellow #F9C42E, cleared-hazard green #75C73E, hazard/pothole brown #8B6F47, camera-alert gray #6B6B6B
- Saturated cartography tokens (louder than a typical map style): warm cream land #FFFCF2, bright cyan water #9BDEEF, mint-green parks #C5E89B, white major roads, warm-white minor roads, a golden highway fill #FFD970
- Canvas/surface: card white #FFFFFF, surface gray #F5F5F7, surface pressed #EAEAEC, divider #D6D6D9
- Text: ink (a warm near-black) #1A1A1A, secondary #6B6B6B, tertiary #A0A0A0
- Dark/night-driving mode: charcoal map land #1E2026, deep teal-navy water #0F3D5E, dark forest park #1F3A1F, card surface #262932 — crucially, BOTH brand colors brighten rather than desaturate: purple to #9F76DA, cyan to #5DD9FF, so the brand stays vivid even at night

TYPE SCALE (a proprietary rounded sans, with a system rounded-design font as the correct fallback — never a sharp grotesque; a monospaced/tabular companion cut for all numerics)
- Hero street name (on a next-turn card): 32pt / 900 (black weight) — the single heaviest weight in the whole system, reserved for this and the speed-limit number
- Next-turn distance (numeric, tabular): 28pt / 700
- Step title: 22pt / 700
- Step subtitle: 17pt / 400
- ETA time (numeric, tabular): 24pt / 700
- Place-card title: 26pt / 700
- Uppercase section header: 13pt / 700, +0.6pt tracking
- Speed-limit number (numeric, tabular): 22pt / 900
- Current-speed number (numeric, tabular): 32pt / 700
- Hazard-bubble title: 14pt / 700
- Button label: 17pt / 700
- Tab label: 10pt / 500

SIGNATURE COMPONENT SPECS
- Cartoon hazard speech bubble — the system's single most recognizable component: a chunky rounded-rectangle (~14pt radius) at full color saturation with a small triangular tail pointing down at the hazard's exact location; a white icon leads a bold title and, optionally, a lighter "reported N minutes ago" timestamp; appears with a spring "pop" (scale from nothing up past full size and settling)
- Floating report button: a 56pt circular FAB in the primary brand purple, bottom-right, carrying a TINTED purple shadow rather than a neutral one (reinforcing brand identity at the app's single most-used action point); tapping opens a circular "report wheel" of 6-8 hazard-category wedges
- Current-location marker: NOT a dot — a chunky arrow/cone shape in the secondary brand color with a bold white outline, rotating to match heading, plus a soft expanding pulse ring behind it
- Next-turn card: a full-width card at the top of the screen in the solid primary brand color, combining a large rotated direction glyph, the tabular distance figure, and the upcoming street name in the heaviest available weight
- Bottom info bar (during active navigation): a persistent bar showing a tabular duration figure, a tabular distance-plus-arrival-time line, an optional "alternate route saves N minutes" pill in the cleared-hazard green, and an end/stop control
- Compact status tile (speed limit + current speed): a small square card showing a circular speed-limit badge above a large current-speed figure that flips to the hazard-red tone the moment the user exceeds the posted limit

SPACING / RADIUS
- 4pt base unit; scale 4-8-12-16-20-24-28-32-40-48-56-64-80
- Radius scale leans deliberately rounder than most travel apps: 8 (card sections) · 12 (status tile, photo cards) · 14 (hazard bubbles, primary containers) · 16 (bottom-sheet top, search field) · 24-28 (pill-style buttons) · circular (the report FAB, mood/status avatars)

MOTION
- Report-button tap: quick scale down and back (roughly 200ms) with the shadow tightening then releasing
- Hazard bubble appearance: a spring "pop" — scale overshoots past full size before settling, around 400ms
- Location-marker pulse: a slow ~2000ms breathing ring, looping infinitely
- Route-line "ant trail": a moving dash pattern animating continuously along the route to signal "this line is live, not static"
- Primary CTA press: a firm scale-down paired with a heavy-weight haptic, followed by a cross-fade into the next mode
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. Never render a hazard or alert as a plain small pin — every alert type gets the full chunky speech-bubble treatment with a pointed tail, because the whole point of a community-reporting feature is that contributing (and seeing others' contributions) feels like play, not paperwork.
2. Keep the current-location marker a directional arrow shape, never a plain circular dot — a dot loses the sense of "which way am I facing," which matters constantly in a driving context, and the arrow is also this brand's clearest visual differentiator from a generic maps app.
3. Don't desaturate the cartography to make it "calmer" — bright water, bright parks, and a golden highway fill are the whole point of a louder, more game-like map; muting them to look like a conventional maps app erases the personality that makes reporting fun.
4. Route every distance, time, speed, and ETA figure through the tabular/monospaced numeric cut — at driving speed, a jittering non-tabular number is actively harder to read than the same number set in fixed-width digits.
5. Reserve the heaviest (black/900) type weight for exactly two moments — the hero street name on the next-turn card and the speed-limit number — using it more broadly dilutes the "this is the one thing you must read right now" signal.
6. Give the primary floating action button and the primary CTA a color-tinted shadow that matches the brand purple, not a neutral gray shadow — a tinted shadow at the app's two highest-frequency touch points reinforces brand identity at exactly the moments users interact most.
7. Keep both brand colors (the primary violet and its cyan counterpart) at full saturation in dark/night mode, only brightening them for legibility rather than desaturating — a night-driving mode that drains the brand colors to gray loses the "still feels like the same app" continuity that matters when someone's been driving for hours.
8. Position the primary floating report action bottom-right and never bottom-left or centered — consistency here matters because users learn its location by muscle memory while driving and glancing down only briefly.
9. Animate a new hazard report's appearance with an overshoot "pop," not a flat fade-in — the small bounce is what makes a report feel like a rewarding, game-like confirmation rather than a neutral data update.
</house_rules>

<the_project>
Describe your own community-driven or gamified navigation/mapping app so this system can be retargeted:
- App name and what your community reports (hazards, points of interest, deals, availability, etc.):
- How many distinct report/alert categories do you need, and what does each represent:
- Primary brand color(s) you want in place of the violet/cyan pair, if different:
- Is turn-by-turn navigation core to the product, or is this more of a map-annotation/discovery app:
- Do you need a speed or pace-tracking readout, or is that not relevant to your use case:
- What should the primary floating action actually do (report something, add a pin, start a session):
- Any constraint on how playful vs. serious the visual tone should be:
</the_project>

<what_to_give_me>
1. Retargeted color tokens — Swift `Color` extensions for your primary brand pair, your report/alert category colors, and a night/dark-mode variant that brightens rather than desaturates the brand colors.
2. The cartoon-style alert/report bubble component — adapted to your real report categories, with the pointed-tail shape and the spring "pop" appearance animation.
3. The primary floating action button — sized and shadowed per the tinted-shadow rule above, plus a circular category picker if you have multiple report types.
4. The current-position/heading marker — a directional shape (not a dot) with a pulsing presence ring.
5. If turn-by-turn is relevant: the next-turn hero card and the bottom info bar, using the tabular numeric type cut throughout.
6. A do's-and-don'ts list (7-9 items) protecting the "reports are chunky and game-like, cartography stays loud, night mode brightens rather than desaturates" rules above.
7. Accessibility notes — Dynamic Type scope (what's fixed for glanceability at speed vs. what scales), VoiceOver phrasing for the alert bubble and the position marker, and a reduced-motion fallback for the pop, pulse, and ant-trail animations.
</what_to_give_me>
install: Paste the prompt into your assistant with your map SDK and navigation state already scaffolded
Fill in <the_project> with your real report categories and how playful you want the tone
Request the hazard-bubble and FAB components first since they anchor the whole reporting loop
Verify both brand colors stay legible (brightened, not desaturated) once your dark/night mode is wired up
